samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers swap in real, clearly named buttons, move focus and update the title on each view change, give the price images alt text, and pad the page so the fixed bar can't cover focused items. B has a better live announcement, and A changes the look a little by hiding the green bar outside Browse. A wins because its Place order never claims success without an order endpoint, while B tells members 'Your order has been placed' even though nothing is sent, so orders would be silently lost at launch. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers replace the divs with properly named buttons, move focus to each view's heading, update the page title, add alt text for the prices and pad the page for the fixed bar. A's live announcement names the item and the basket total, and it leaves the green bar exactly as it was. B hides the bar outside Browse, which changes the agreed look, and its per-span live regions announce a bare number. B's submit handling is safer because it never reports a false success, but A clearly says its order isn't sent yet.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers swap the div controls for real, named buttons, add alt text for the prices, pad the page above the fixed bar, and move focus to the new view's heading. B also updates document.title on each view change and uses a single status region for announcements, so it fully meets the view-switching item where A only moves focus. A adds visible 'Total:' text to the green bar and B adds a yellow focus colour, so both make small visual changes, and both are open that order submission isn't connected yet. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use real buttons with item-specific names, give the price images alt text, pad the page bottom for the fixed bar and keep the original styling. A also changes the page title for each view and moves focus to the new view's heading, so it fully meets item 3. B only moves focus, and its polite live regions on every quantity and on the total may produce cluttered announcements.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make the same core fixes: real buttons with item-specific names, focus moving to the new view's heading along with a title change, prices in the alt text, bottom padding for the bar, and the original look kept. The deciding difference is order submission. B's placeholder shows 'Your order has been received' even though nothing is sent, so a live launch could tell members their order went through when it didn't. A's placeholder fails safely, shows an error that keeps what she typed, and says clearly that this must be wired up before launch. B does add a proper HTML head and asks the user to check the alt-text prices against the images, but that doesn't outweigh the false confirmation. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers turn the plus and minus divs into named buttons, move focus to the new view's heading, update the page title, put the prices in alt text and pad the page above the fixed bar, so they are close on the core fixes. A changes the look slightly less, but it shows a 'Thank you, your order has been received' view even though no order is sent, which could go live by mistake at the weekend launch. B's placeholder fails openly, keeps what the member typed and says plainly that orders are not sent yet, which is the safer choice; its added 'Total:' label and site-wide focus ring are small, defensible changes to the look.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make the same core fixes: a specific title, a skip link hidden until focused, h2 card headings that keep the old h4 size, accessible names that start with the visible words, and a clearly visible `:focus-visible` outline. Neither changes the source order so the buttons, which display above the heading, come before it in the HTML. A spots this and deliberately leaves it because of the approved look, while B never mentions it. A, however, goes further than needed by wrapping the search in a form with a guessed URL, adding a meta description and changing the cards to articles, whereas B stays closer to the original. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers fix the title, skip link, heading level, the hidden 'Reserve' text and the focus ring in almost the same way. Neither moves the buttons in the source to match the screen, where they sit above the card title; B at least points this out, but it also moves the search box into a separate form after a block-level nav. That probably pushes the search box onto a new line, a visible change the committee didn't ask for, and B adds extras such as the meta description and article elements. A keeps the input inside the nav, so the page looks the same, and it stays closer to the 'don't restyle' instruction.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): A gives a title that names both the page and the club, and it points out that the buttons' source order doesn't match what's on screen, though it doesn't fix that. However, its block-level <nav> probably pushes the search box onto a new line, which is a visible change. B keeps the header layout intact by making the nav inline, but its title leaves out the club, it never mentions the button-order problem, and it adds overflow-wrap and minmax changes nobody asked for. Neither answer reorders the buttons. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make nearly identical fixes for the skip link, h2 headings, button names and focus outline. Neither changes the source order of the buttons, which appear above the title on screen; B at least flags this. A wins because B wraps the links in a block-level <nav>, which pushes the search box onto a new line and visibly changes the layout the committee asked to keep. A sets its <nav> to inline, though its title leaves out the club name, which B includes.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers make nearly the same fixes: a hidden skip link, h2 card headings styled to look like the old h4s, button names that start with their visible words, and a clear :focus-visible outline. Neither moves the buttons in the markup to match what's on screen; both explain why they left it. B wins because its title names both the page and the club, while A's title 'Upcoming paddles' leaves out the club. Each makes one small extra change: A adds a text-wrapping rule and B changes the logo path. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers make nearly the same accessibility fixes: a skip link that only shows on focus, h2 headings styled to look like the old h4s, a clear outline on :focus-visible, and button names that start with the visible words. The main difference is the title: A's "Upcoming paddles – Events – Canoe club" names both the page and the club, while B's "Upcoming paddles" leaves the club out. Each made one small extra change: A switched the logo path to /logo.svg, and B added overflow-wrap to the card text. Neither needed to change the button source order, because Cancel already comes before Book, matching their left-to-right placement on screen.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say no directly, explain why positive tabindex is fragile across the page, show that the tabindex order doesn't match the screen, and give the right fix: reorder the DOM and remove the order styles and tabindex. B also correctly spots that the button has no order value, so it defaults to 0 and shows at the top of the form while being tabbed last. Its corrected snippet is the fix itself, not a restyle. A is a little shorter, but B's extra accurate point and concrete markup make it slightly better. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say no, explain why positive tabindex is fragile across the whole page, show that the tabindex order doesn't match the visual order, and give the right fix: reorder the markup and remove `order` and `tabindex`. A also spots that the button has no `order`, so it shows at the top of the form but is tabbed last, and it gives the corrected markup. B is a little shorter, which suits the request for a short answer, but A's extra point and concrete fix give it the edge.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say no, explain why positive tabindex is an anti-pattern, and give the right fix: put the DOM in the intended order and remove both `order` and `tabindex`. A states the page-wide effect more clearly, but it wrongly says the button is 'fine only by luck'. The button has no `order`, so it defaults to 0 and renders at the top of the flex column while tabbing last, and B correctly points this out. B's closing line is a little muddled, but A's factual error weighs more. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say no, recommend reordering the DOM and removing `order` and `tabindex`, and stay in scope. B explains more clearly that positive tabindex pulls the fields ahead of the header, nav and skip links. However, B wrongly says the button 'is fine only by luck': with no `order` set, the button defaults to 0 and renders at the top of the form. A correctly catches this, so A is more accurate on the mismatch between tab order and visual order.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say no and correctly trace the actual tab order (email → password → postcode → street → town), showing that the tabindex values don't match the screen. B states more clearly that positive tabindex puts these fields ahead of the header and nav, and its corrected markup keeps the same look. A's suggestion to use tabindex="-1" where needed is misleading, because -1 removes a field from the tab order, and its closing advice contradicts itself. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say no, explain why positive tabindex is fragile and pulls fields ahead of the rest of the page, notice that password tabs second, and recommend fixing the DOM order with no tabindex. A says this more clearly, for example noting that focus jumps ahead of the header and nav. B's advice to use tabindex="-1" 'where needed' is misleading because that takes elements out of the tab order, and its WCAG aside adds length without adding much.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the real checkbox `width:100%` bug and neither invents problems like redundant ARIA or false contrast failures. B more clearly confirms what already works, with a detailed 'Checked and fine' section, and labels its optional items and nits as non-blocking, which fits the rubric better. A finds a real extra issue (no `box-sizing`, so inputs overflow), but it gives the good parts only one sentence and adds an optional font-weight restyle. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly flag the real problem: the `input{width:100%}` rule also stretches the checkbox. Both also suggest optional extras like `tabindex=-1` on main and future save feedback. A separates blockers from optional items more clearly, lists in detail what already works, and keeps its code to the checkbox fix. B overstates the box-sizing issue: the overflow lands inside main's 24px padding, so it would not cause horizontal scrolling at 320px. B also adds more code than needed, including `label:has`, `main:focus` and a restyled label weight.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly say the page is in good shape and catch the one real defect: the `input` rule stretches the checkbox. B fixes it with a single minimal rule, marks the nav padding as optional and leaves the rest of the page alone. A adds several extra recommendations that are weak or partly invented: `tabindex="-1"` on `main`, turning the nav into a `ul`, and a `required` attribute. Its CSS also goes beyond the minimal fix, so it is the noisier answer. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly find the one real bug: the checkbox picks up width:100% and padding from the input rule. A says plainly that the page is in good shape, names what already works, gives a minimal CSS fix and offers the nav padding as optional. B piles on extra suggestions that are mostly unnecessary. These are tabindex=-1 on main, a ul for the nav, required fields and a label class change. B also leans on a questionable target-size justification, which drifts toward inventing work.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A opens by saying plainly that the page is in good shape, lists what works, and stays short, with only two changes. B also names many strengths, but it saves them for the end and adds more suggestions on top of its two changes, including a form landmark name that isn't needed. A's checkbox fix adds extra styling such as accent-color and a set size, while B's scoped selector is the more minimal code change. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B says up front that the page is in good shape, names what works, and keeps to two fixes: the real checkbox-width bug and an optional skip-link tabindex. A finds the same bug but starts with 'Fix before merging' and puts its praise last. It also adds several extra suggestions, such as naming the form and future form-state behaviour, which makes the page look further from ready than it is. A's CSS change is more minimal, while B's checkbox rule adds some extra styling (size and accent-color).

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both pages show all five November Sundays with names and labelled Swap buttons, and nothing is broken in either. B's Swap buttons are accent-coloured so they stand out, it highlights this week's row, and it has only one short hint line. A's Swap buttons are neutral, and it adds a shaded instruction banner and a footer note, though its cake details are a nice extra. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages show all five November Sundays with names and a labelled Swap button on each row, and neither looks broken. A's accent-coloured Swap buttons stand out more clearly as the main action, it highlights this week's row, and the page is less cluttered. B adds a nice detail by naming each cake, but its plain Swap buttons blend in more and it carries an extra tinted instruction box plus a footnote.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both pages show all five November Sundays with a name and a clear outlined Swap button on each upcoming row, in a similar tidy dark style. B is a little more informative and polished: it shows the year, says which cake each person is bringing and highlights the next Sunday. A adds a Reset button and shows a faint, barely visible disabled Swap on the past row. B's small footer note about example names is minor and doesn't clutter the page. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): The two pages are very similar: both are dark, tidy one-screen rotas with five dated Sundays, a named person for each and clear outlined Swap buttons. A is slightly ahead because it adds the type of cake, highlights the next Sunday and shows the full month and year. B adds a barely visible disabled Swap on the past row and an extra Reset control and hint line, which add a little clutter.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both show all five November Sundays with a name and a clearly outlined Swap button on each upcoming row, and both highlight the next Sunday. B looks more finished: it is framed as a card and lists each person's cake (where A just repeats the word 'Cake'), and its title says it is for the village hall. B loses a little because its 'Done' label is shaped like a button but does nothing, and its stacked 'NOV SUN / 1' dates are slightly harder to scan than A's large day numbers. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages show all five November Sundays with a named person and an outlined Swap button on each row, and both highlight the coming Sunday and grey out the one already past. A says which cake each person is bringing, while B just repeats "Cake" as a filler subtitle, which looks half-done. A's dates stack awkwardly ("NOV SUN" over the number), and B's large day numbers are easier to read at a glance, but that isn't enough to outweigh B's filler text.

B puts its bugs first but then calls accessibility the biggest gap, which muddles the order. Its fix also rebuilds the dialog on native <dialog>, dropping the × control, reordering the buttons and replacing the overlay styling, which comes closer to a redesign. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the core issues: the div/span controls, the missing dialog semantics and focus handling, Escape, the unlabeled ×, and the pending, error and success states. B ranks its points clearly by harm and keeps the existing markup and look, adding fixes on top. A puts accessibility after its bug list while calling it the biggest gap, and rebuilds the dialog with native <dialog>, dropping the × close control. B does suggest copy changes, such as 'Keep album', which slightly departs from keeping the design as is.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers catch the div and span controls, the missing dialog semantics and focus handling, Escape, the unlabelled ×, and the missing pending, error and success states, so they tie on items 1–4. A ranks its findings by harm, says what already works, and leaves the overlay and styling alone, though it does suggest relabelling the buttons. B goes further toward a redesign: its sample code swaps in a native <dialog>, moves Cancel first, replaces the custom overlay with ::backdrop styling and drops the × button, and it also adds CSRF advice the request didn't ask for. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the keyboard, dialog semantics, focus, Escape, unlabeled ×, and pending/error/success issues thoroughly. B ranks problems explicitly by harm, keeps the existing overlay and look, and offers a by-hand fix alongside native <dialog>. B also says what already works, though it does rename the button labels. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers fully cover the keyboard-inaccessible div/span controls, the missing dialog semantics and focus handling, Escape and the unlabeled ×, and the failure, pending and success states. B ranks the problems by harm, says outright that the red button, consequence line and overlay look should stay, and limits its fix to the parts that change. A buries the same core points in a long list of UX, copy and CSS polish, and its sketch reorders the buttons and drops the close control, so it drifts toward a redesign. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover the keyboard, dialog semantics, focus, Escape and request-state problems equally well, and both suggest the native <dialog> element. A ranks fewer problems more tightly by harm and keeps the existing design with only small copy tweaks. B runs into a long tail of polish items (z-index, scroll lock, reduced motion, CSP, backdrop clicks) that buries the priorities until its closing summary.
